READING PASSAGE 3
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3
on pages 10 and 11.
Reading Greek
A foreword to a textbook of Classical Greek, which, together with Latin, was for
centuries an important part of the school curriculum in many European
countries
There is only one criterion by which a course for learners of a dead language, that is a
language no longer spoken, should be judged: the efficiency and speed with which it brings
them to the stage of reading texts in the original language with precision, understanding and
enjoyment. The setting up of the Greek Project by the Joint Association of Classical Teachers
(JACT) was the product of a conviction that it was possible to compose a course in ancient
Greek which would satisfy that criterion substantially better than any course in existence.
There would have been little point in such a project if the current decline in the study of
Classical Greek in schools had clearly reflected a growing and irreversible failure on the part
of modern society to respond aesthetically and intellectually to Greek culture. But there has
been no such failure of response, for the popularity of Classical Greek literature in
translation, and of adult education courses in Greek art and history, has continued to increase.
It seemed to the Joint Association that there was a gap waiting to be bridged. Such a venture
would need funding. and when an appeal for £40,000 was launched it was legitimate to
wonder how the cause of Classical Greek would fare in competition with louder claims. But
the optimists were justified: within a few months, £63,000 had been contributed, and two
years later an appeal for the money required for a fourth and final year of work brought in
more than £15,000.
When the project began. it would not have been difficult for the JACT writers to compile yet
another systematic grammar book of Classical Greek and interweave it with exercises which
would test the learners’ progress through grammar, stage by stage. Nor would it have been
difficult to confront the learners with an anthology of Classical Greek literature, translate
most of it for them, offering some grammatical rules from time to time, in order to inspire
them with the hope that they would get the hang of the language and eventually pick up the
“gist’ or the ‘essentials’ of any Classical Greek text. Anyone who learns Classical Greek by
the first of those two ways will take a very long time to reach the point of reading a genuine
text; on the way they will have acquired much more grammatical knowledge than they need,
and much less knowledge than they need of ancient Greek thought and feeling. The technique
of compiling a descriptive grammar for reference purposes, and that of introducing learners to
a language are utterly different, as teachers of modern languages know.
Equally, the notion that one can get the gist of alien texts simply by reading a lot of them with
the help of translations, but without careful linguistic guidance, is just as illusory. We can
indeed hope to understand much of what is said to us in a modern language if we are put into
an environment in which we hear it every day, but our progress depends on our being a
participant in the situation in which the words are uttered, and on the readiness of the native
speaker to repeat, simplify, slow down and supplement language by signs and gestures. Our

11
relationship to Classical Greek authors is different: if we tackle philosophical arguments or
tragic dialogue with only a hazy idea of grammar, the chances of misunderstanding — not
marginal, but total misunderstanding — are very high.
The Greek Project course has been written and scrutinised by people who care most about
what works best, and who do not use ‘traditional’ or “modern” as complimentary or
derogatory terms. In the earlier sections, the most common words and constructions
predominate, and the sentences are short; however, the sentence structure has not been
anglicised. and the test of frequency has not been so rigorously applied to the admission of
vocabulary and idiom as to bleach all colour out of the language. At the start of the course the
Greek texts have been specially written, though the ideas were taken from Greek sources; the
voices of Plato and Aristophanes* soon begin to be heard, and thereafter, the specially written
texts are edged out as the ancient authors, progressively less adapted to suit the beginner's
limitations, take over. The content of the text is determined as seldom as possible by
linguistic tidiness, and as often as possible by the need to acquaint the adult and near-adult
learners directly with the characteristic features of Classical Greek culture.
Not all language experts think that it is right to make up texts in this way, or to adapt original
texts. There is nothing in any language course that everyone thinks is right. The JACT team
has been repeatedly compelled to take decisions — sometimes against the judgement of a
minority, but never without patient and friendly discussion — which will incur criticism.
Critics are asked to reflect that the combined classroom, lecture room and tutorial experience
of the group is not only considerable, but very varied — the JACT project team tested out
successive drafts of the course on students and constantly revised them in the light of what
emerged from the testing — and that in language learning. occasions may arise where one
person’s delicious dish is another person’s cold cabbage.
The team has produced a course which they have many good reasons to believe will prove,
for the majority of learners, a straighter and shorter path than any other into Classical Greek
literature as the ancient Greeks themselves knew it.
* Plato and Aristophanes: two famous Greek writers of ancient times

Questions 27 — 30
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 27-30 on your answer sheet.
27 In the second paragraph, the writer states that the study of Greek literature and
history is
A regarded by many as outdated.
B still common in many schools.
c in demand by the general public.
D more expensive than other courses.
28 In the fourth paragraph, the writer states that reading classical texts
A is made easier by a knowledge of other languages.
B takes more time than reading in a modern language.
c requires the same skills as reading a modern text.
D requires an adequate knowledge of grammar.
29 In the fifth paragraph, the statement that the JACT writers took care not to ‘bleach all
colour out of the language’ means that they wanted to
A avoid offensive words or phrases.
B make the texts suit a wide range of students.
c preserve the original feel of Classical Greek.
D make it difficult enough to challenge more advanced students.
30 Which of the following best sums up the purpose of this passage?
A to persuade more schools to offer Classical Greek
B to convince readers of the value of the new Classical Greek course
c to argue that modern languages are more useful than dead ones
D to outline the difficulties of learning classical languages
